title: Learning before breakfast
hook: the day begins with a blessing over Torah, then a little study straight away

segments.voice: Yesterday, peah and deeds without measure, the list of things with no ceiling. Your line was no limit on kindness. Did you do the deed you pictured? Today, the blessing that comes just before that list. Day five hundred forty-eight.

A lot of mornings start by taking something in. Headlines. Messages. Somebody else's photos of somebody else's breakfast. Whatever comes first tends to set the weather for the rest of the morning. The Jewish prayer book has an opinion about what should come first. Very early, before the psalms, before the main prayers, before a single request, there's a blessing for studying Torah. And then, so the blessing isn't left hanging in the air, a few lines to actually study, right there, on the spot.
screen: `WHATEVER COMES FIRST SETS THE WEATHER.` → `A BLESSING FOR STUDY.` → `THEN STUDY, ON THE SPOT.`

segments.voice: The blessing comes from the Talmud, tractate Berakhot, where several rabbis each offer their own wording, and the prayer book keeps more than one. The first thanks God who commanded us la'asok b'divrei Torah, to busy ourselves with the words of Torah. Not just to read, or to finish, but to be busy with it, the way you're busy with work. The next asks: make the words of Torah sweet in our mouths, and in the mouths of our children and their children. Sweet, the way honey is sweet. And the last is the one the Talmud calls the finest of blessings: who chose us and gave us the Torah. Then comes the part that makes the morning feel like a classroom. Right after the blessing, the prayer book gives a few lines to study, so the blessing has something to bless. In many prayer books, the first lines are the priestly blessing from the Book of Numbers, in the old Jewish translation: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee." Then the lists you heard about yesterday, from the Mishnah and the Talmud. A verse of Torah, a mishnah, a passage of Talmud: a taste of each layer of the tradition. The Talmud takes this blessing seriously. In tractate Nedarim, it even suggests that when learned people's children didn't become learned, it was because their parents hadn't blessed the Torah first. Study, in this telling, isn't only information. It's meant to be received as a gift, with thanks, before you open it.
screen: `TO BUSY OURSELVES WITH TORAH.` · `MAKE THE WORDS SWEET.` · `THEN A FEW LINES, RIGHT AWAY.` · `RECEIVED AS A GIFT, WITH THANKS.` · then, large: `LEARN SOMETHING FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say a blessing, then read one line. Settle, and breathe. Pick up something worth learning from: a page of scripture, a book you trust, even the line in today's lesson. If you pray, you can first say the blessing's own words, la'asok b'divrei Torah, to busy ourselves with the words of Torah. If you don't, take one breath of thanks for being able to read at all. Then read one line, slowly, twice. Let it be the first thing you take in today, ahead of the news. The bell holds the time.
Divrei Torah. Words of Torah — the morning blessing asks to be busy with them, then the prayer book gives a few lines to study on the spot.
Your line: learn something first. Today, before you open the next app, read one line of something worth learning, and tomorrow, do it first thing. Day five hundred forty-eight.

screen: `DAY 548 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BINDING IN THE MORNING.`

howItsDone: Jews who pray each morning say the blessings over the Torah early in the service, then immediately read a few short passages, often the priestly blessing, a mishnah and a passage of Talmud, so the blessing covers the day's study.

original.note: Hebrew: to busy ourselves with the words of Torah, from the morning blessing.

trapdoor: what you thought: a formal blessing before a reading.
what it means: each morning, study is received as a gift, blessed, and begun at once, before anything else is taken in.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 11b records several wordings, combined in the siddur; Nedarim 81a ties the failure to bless the Torah first to learning not passing to the next generation.

sources.quoted: The LORD bless thee, and keep thee

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'a verse, a law, a story' was inaccurate for the study passages; now 'a verse of Torah, a mishnah, a passage of Talmud'. The practice no longer confuses the priestly blessing with the Torah blessing. Softened 'most of us'; the carry now starts today.

Berakhot 11b: the several wordings (la'asok b'divrei Torah; veha'arev na; asher bachar banu, called 'the finest of blessings' by Rav Hamnuna); confirm attributions and the claim that the siddur combines them (Ashkenazi practice; some rites differ on la'asok vs al divrei Torah).
Study passages after the blessings: priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24–26), Mishnah Peah 1:1, Shabbat 127a in many Ashkenazi siddurim; Sephardi rites differ. Confirm.
Nedarim 81a: why scholars' children are not scholars, 'because they did not bless the Torah first'; confirm.
